subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Authority Bias
description: A 60-second lesson on The Authority Bias.

hook.text: Hospital nurses gave dangerous drug doses because a doctor ordered it by phone. No questions asked.

buildup.text: Milgram's experiment showed 65% of people delivered what they believed were lethal shocks on orders.

discovery.text: Authority bias: we obey and trust authority figures even when their instructions conflict with reason.

twist.text: A lab coat alone increases compliance. The authority doesn't need real expertise, just the appearance.

climax.text: Healthy skepticism means evaluating the argument, not the title. Credentials don't guarantee correctness.

quiz.question: What increases compliance in authority bias?
options: Even superficial symbols of authority like a lab coat

details.summary: Authority bias is the tendency to attribute greater accuracy and credibility to the opinions of authority figures regardless of whether their authority is relevant to the topic. People defer to experts, titles, and uniforms even in domains outside the authority's expertise.
details.whyItMatters: Authority bias is exploited by marketing using doctor endorsements for non-medical products, by organizations silencing dissent from junior staff who may have better information, and by society accepting claims from credentialed people without.
takeaways: People defer to authority even when the authority is irrelevant to the topic
Milgram's experiments demonstrated extreme obedience to authority figures
Authority bias suppresses valuable dissent from less credentialed individuals

faq.question: How does authority bias affect decision-making in organizations?
faq.answer: Junior employees with better local knowledge defer to senior managers who lack context. Medical teams follow incorrect senior physician orders. The hierarchy's authority structure overrides the actual information distribution.

faq.question: How can authority bias be reduced?
faq.answer: Anonymous input systems, flat decision-making structures, asking junior members to speak first in meetings, and evaluating ideas on merit rather than source all help. The key is separating the credibility of the idea from the status of the speaker.
